title: Start here: investing from zero
intro: New to investing? Start here. In 24 short lessons you'll go from 'what is a stock?' to reading company numbers and building smart habits, with a quick quiz after each one. It's education, not advice, and you can go at your own pace.

units.title: Money basics
units.blurb: The foundations: saving, growth, inflation, safety nets and risk.

lessons.title: Saving vs investing
lessons.hook: Saving keeps money safe. Investing puts it to work. You need both, for different jobs.

sections.heading: Two jobs for your money
body: **Saving** means setting money aside somewhere safe and easy to reach, like a bank savings account. The amount you put in stays the same or grows a little from interest. It is there when you need it.

**Investing** means buying something you expect to grow in value over time, like a small piece of a company (a share) or a fund that holds many companies. It can grow much more than savings, but its value goes up and down, sometimes a lot.

sections.heading: When to use which
body: A simple way to decide: think about when you will need the money. Money for the next few years (rent, a car repair, a trip next summer) usually belongs in savings, because you cannot afford for it to drop 20% right when you need it.

Money you will not touch for many years (retirement, a goal ten years away) has time to ride out the ups and downs. That is where investing makes sense for many people. The longer you can wait, the more the bumps tend to smooth out, though there is never a guarantee.

sections.heading: A note before you start
body: This course is education, not personal advice. It explains how things work and what the trade-offs are. It will never tell you to buy a particular stock or fund. Your situation, goals and country matter, so for big decisions consider talking to a qualified, fee-only financial professional.

example.title: Two pots, two jobs
body: Sam has $3,000. Sam keeps $1,500 in savings for surprises and puts $1,500 into an investment fund for the long term.

If the fund drops 20% in a bad year, the investment is worth $1,200 for a while. Annoying, but Sam does not have to sell, because the $1,500 in savings covers any surprise. The savings pot protects the investing pot.

key_terms.definition: Keeping money somewhere safe and easy to reach. Low risk, low growth.
Buying assets like shares or funds that you expect to grow over time. Higher potential growth, but the value can fall.
How long until you need the money. It is one of the biggest factors in choosing between saving and investing.

lessons.takeaway: Save for the near future, invest for the far future.
lessons.try_it: Reflection: list one goal you have for the next two years and one for ten or more years from now. Which pot does each belong in?

quiz.question: Maya needs $2,000 for a course that starts in four months. Where does that money most sensibly belong?
options: In the stock market, because it grows faster
In savings, because she needs it soon and cannot risk a drop
It doesn't matter, the outcome is the same
quiz.explanation: With a four-month time horizon there is no time to recover from a fall, so a safe, easy-to-reach place fits the job.

quiz.question: Why can investing make more sense for money you won't need for 15 years?
options: Banks charge fees on long-term savings
Savings accounts are not allowed to hold money that long
Long time horizons give room to ride out ups and downs
quiz.explanation: A long horizon doesn't remove risk, but it gives you time to wait through bad years instead of being forced to sell.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the difference between saving and investing?
options: Saving is for rich people, investing is for everyone
They are the same thing with different names
Investing guarantees a higher return than saving
Saving prioritises safety and access; investing accepts ups and downs for more growth potential
quiz.explanation: Investing offers more growth potential, not a guarantee. Saving trades growth for safety and easy access.

lessons.title: Compound growth: money that grows on itself
lessons.hook: Why starting early matters more than starting big.

sections.heading: Growth on top of growth
body: When your money earns a return, that return gets added to your balance. Next year you earn a return on the bigger balance, including last year's gains. That is **compound growth**: growth on top of growth.
Think of a snowball rolling downhill. At first it picks up a little snow. As it gets bigger, each turn picks up more, because there is more surface to stick to.

sections.heading: Time does the heavy lifting
body: In the early years compounding looks boring. The magic shows up later, because the base you are growing keeps getting bigger. That is why time is often more powerful than the amount you start with.

A handy shortcut is the **Rule of 72**: divide 72 by the yearly growth rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 6% a year, that is about 12 years. At 9%, about 8 years. It is an approximation, not an exact answer.

sections.heading: The honest fine print
body: Real investments do not grow by a neat, fixed percentage every year. Some years are up a lot, some are down. The numbers in this lesson are illustrative averages to show the idea, not a promise. Compounding also works against you with debt: credit card interest compounds too.

example.title: $100 growing at 7% a year (illustrative)
body: Year 1: $100 earns $7, so you have $107. Year 2: you earn 7% of $107, which is $7.49, so you have $114.49.
Keep going and after 10 years you have about $197. After 20 years, about $387. After 30 years, about $761.
Notice the pattern: the first 10 years add about $97, but the last 10 years (from year 20 to 30) add about $374. Same rate, same starting $100. The difference is the bigger base.

key_terms.definition: Earning returns on both your original money and the returns it has already earned.
A quick estimate: 72 divided by the yearly growth rate is roughly the number of years for money to double.
How much an investment gains or loses, usually shown as a percentage per year.

lessons.takeaway: Compounding rewards time, so starting early, even small, can beat starting big later.
lessons.try_it: In paper trading, note your starting $10,000. Use the Rule of 72 to estimate how long it would take to double at an illustrative 8% a year.

quiz.question: Using the Rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double at 6% a year?
quiz.explanation: 72 divided by 6 is 12, so about 12 years. It is an estimate, not an exact figure.

quiz.question: $100 grows at 10% a year. How much is it worth after two years?
quiz.explanation: Year one gives $110. Year two adds 10% of $110, which is $11, for $121. The extra $1 is compounding.

quiz.question: Why do the later years of compounding add more dollars than the early years at the same rate?
options: Interest rates always rise over time
Banks pay bonuses to long-term customers
The balance being grown is larger, so the same percentage is more dollars
quiz.explanation: A fixed percentage of a bigger number is a bigger number. That growing base is the heart of compounding.

lessons.title: Inflation: why cash slowly shrinks
lessons.hook: A $20 bill under your mattress loses value every year without you noticing.

sections.heading: Prices creep up
body: **Inflation** is the general rise in prices over time. If a sandwich costs $10 this year and $10.30 next year, that is 3% inflation for sandwiches. When inflation is 3%, your same dollar buys about 3% less stuff each year.

In the US, inflation is commonly measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which tracks the price of a basket of everyday goods and services. The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, aims for inflation of about 2% a year over time. Many other countries' central banks have similar targets.

sections.heading: Real vs nominal
body: A **nominal** return is the number you see. A **real** return is what is left after inflation. If your savings account pays 2% and inflation is 3%, your balance goes up, but your buying power goes down by roughly 1%.
That is the hidden cost of keeping long-term money in cash. It feels safe, because the number never drops. But its buying power can quietly shrink.

sections.heading: What this means for you
body: Cash is still the right tool for short-term needs and emergencies. Inflation is mostly a problem for money you will hold for many years. That is one reason people invest long-term money in things that have historically tended to grow faster than inflation, accepting more ups and downs in exchange.

example.title: $1,000 at 3% inflation (illustrative)
body: If prices rise 3% a year, something that costs $1,000 today would cost about $1,344 in 10 years.

Flip it around: $1,000 kept in cash would buy only about 74% as much after 10 years. Using the Rule of 72, at 3% inflation prices roughly double in 24 years, which means cash loses about half its buying power over that time.

key_terms.definition: The general rise in prices over time, which reduces what each dollar can buy.
Your return after subtracting inflation. It measures the change in buying power.
Consumer Price Index, a common US measure of inflation based on prices of everyday goods and services.

lessons.takeaway: Cash that earns less than inflation keeps its number but loses its buying power.
lessons.try_it: Open the glossary and look up 'inflation' and 'real return'. Then think of one thing you buy that costs noticeably more than it did a few years ago.

quiz.question: Your savings pay 1% a year and inflation is 4%. What happens to your buying power?
quiz.explanation: Your balance rises 1%, but prices rise 4%, so you can buy roughly 3% less.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a nominal and a real return?
options: Real returns ignore taxes; nominal returns include them
Nominal is the headline number; real is what's left after inflation
Real returns only apply to property
quiz.explanation: The real return adjusts the headline return for rising prices, so it shows your change in buying power.

quiz.question: Why is inflation a bigger concern for long-term money than for an emergency fund?
options: Emergency funds are protected from inflation by law
Inflation only happens in some years
Over many years small yearly losses in buying power add up a lot
quiz.explanation: A few percent a year matters little over months, but compounds into a large loss of buying power over decades.

resources.title: Why does the Federal Reserve aim for inflation of 2 percent over the longer run?

lessons.title: Emergency fund first, and where to keep it
lessons.hook: Before you invest a dollar, build a cushion. Here are the safe places to park it.

sections.heading: Why a cushion comes first
body: An **emergency fund** is cash set aside for surprises: a job loss, a medical bill, a broken laptop. A common guideline is three to six months of essential expenses, though the right amount depends on how stable your income is.

It comes before investing because investments can be down exactly when life goes wrong. Without a cushion you might have to sell at a loss or use a high-interest credit card. If you carry high-interest debt, paying it down is often part of this foundation too.

sections.heading: Safe places for cash
body: **High-yield savings accounts** are bank accounts that usually pay more interest than a standard savings account, and you can withdraw any time. **CDs** (certificates of deposit) pay a fixed rate if you leave money for a set term, like 12 months, with a penalty for early withdrawal.

**Treasury bills** are short-term loans to the US government, lasting a year or less. They are considered among the safest assets in the world, and their interest is exempt from state and local income tax (though not federal tax). **Money-market funds** are investment funds that hold very short-term, high-quality debt and most aim to keep a steady $1 share price. They are very low risk, but not guaranteed. Rates on all of these change over time, so compare current rates yourself.

sections.heading: What insurance does and doesn't cover
body: **FDIC** insurance protects deposits at US banks, up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, if the bank fails. Credit unions have similar NCUA coverage. It does not cover stocks, bonds, crypto or money-market funds, even if you bought them through a bank.

**SIPC** protects you if your brokerage firm fails and your assets go missing, generally up to $500,000 including up to $250,000 in cash. It does not protect you from investments losing value. Other countries have their own deposit-insurance schemes with different limits.

example.title: Sizing a cushion
body: Alex's essential monthly costs: rent $1,200, food $400, transport $150, phone and utilities $250. That is $2,000 a month.

Three months is $6,000; six months is $12,000. Alex's job is steady, so Alex aims for $6,000, saving $500 a month. That takes 12 months. Alex keeps it in a high-yield savings account so it is safe, insured and reachable.

key_terms.definition: Cash set aside for unexpected expenses, often three to six months of essential costs.
US government protection for bank deposits if a bank fails, up to set limits. It does not cover investments.
Protection if a US brokerage firm fails. It does not cover losses from investments falling in value.
A short-term loan to the US government, lasting a year or less.

lessons.takeaway: Build a cash cushion in a safe, insured place before putting money at risk.
lessons.try_it: Add up your essential monthly costs and multiply by three. That is a starting target for your cushion. Then look up 'FDIC' in the glossary.

quiz.question: Your brokerage firm goes out of business and some of your shares are missing from your account. What is designed to help?
quiz.explanation: SIPC covers missing assets when a member brokerage fails, up to its limits. FDIC covers bank deposits, not brokerage accounts.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT covered by FDIC insurance, even if bought at a bank?
quiz.explanation: Money-market funds are investments, not deposits, so FDIC does not cover them, even though they are very low risk.

quiz.question: Why does an emergency fund usually come before investing?
options: Emergency funds earn higher returns than stocks
So you aren't forced to sell investments, possibly at a loss, when surprises hit
quiz.explanation: A cushion lets your investments stay put through bad times instead of being sold at the worst moment.

resources.title: Are My Deposit Accounts Insured by the FDIC?

lessons.title: Risk and return: two sides of one coin
lessons.hook: Higher potential reward almost always comes with a bumpier ride.

sections.heading: No free lunch
body: In investing, **risk** usually means uncertainty: the chance that your result is very different from what you expected, including losing money. **Return** is what you gain or lose.

The core idea: investments that offer higher potential returns usually come with more risk. If something offered high returns with no risk, everyone would buy it until the price rose and the return disappeared. So anyone promising high returns with no risk deserves suspicion.

sections.heading: A ladder of risk
body: Picture a ladder. At the bottom: insured savings and Treasury bills, with low, steady returns. In the middle: bonds, which usually swing less than stocks. Near the top: a broad mix of stocks. At the very top: single stocks, crypto and other speculative bets, which can soar or crash.

Over the long run, US stocks have returned **roughly 7% a year after inflation on average**, with big swings and no guarantee. Treat that as an illustrative figure, not a forecast. The S&P 500 fell more than 50% from its 2007 peak to its 2009 low, and about a third in a few weeks in early 2020. Average returns hide years like those.

sections.heading: Your risk is personal
body: How much risk makes sense depends on your time horizon, how stable your income is and how you would feel and act if your investments dropped 30%. Someone who would panic and sell at the bottom may be better off with a calmer mix they can stick with.

example.title: Same average, different ride (illustrative)
body: Investment A earns 5% every year. Investment B earns +25%, then -15%, alternating.
Start with $1,000. After two years, A has $1,000 x 1.05 x 1.05 = $1,102.50. B goes to $1,250, then down 15% to $1,062.50.
B's simple average is 5% a year, the same as A, yet B ends with less. Big swings drag on results, and they test your nerves.

key_terms.definition: The uncertainty of an investment's outcome, including the chance of losing money.
How much and how quickly an investment's price moves up and down.
How much ups and downs you can handle, both financially and emotionally, without abandoning your plan.

lessons.takeaway: Higher potential return comes with higher risk; anyone offering one without the other is a red flag.
lessons.try_it: Check the Market mood gauge on today's page. Ask yourself: if your investments dropped 30% on a fearful day, what would you honestly do?

quiz.question: Someone offers an investment with 'high returns and zero risk'. What does this lesson suggest?
options: It's a great opportunity if you act fast
It is a red flag, because risk and return usually go together
It is normal for government bonds
quiz.explanation: If high returns came without risk, prices would adjust until they didn't. Claims like this are a classic warning sign.

quiz.question: Which is generally lowest on the risk ladder?
quiz.explanation: Treasury bills are short-term loans to the US government and are considered among the safest assets.

quiz.question: Two investments have the same simple average return, but one swings much more. What usually happens?
options: The swinging one ends up with less money over time
They always end with the same amount
The swinging one always ends with more
quiz.explanation: Losses hurt more than equal-sized gains help, so bigger swings tend to drag down long-run results.

units.title: How the stock market works
units.blurb: Shares, trading, indexes and why prices move the way they do.

lessons.title: What is a share?
lessons.hook: Owning a share means owning a tiny slice of a real company.

sections.heading: A slice of the pie
body: A company can be split into millions or billions of equal pieces called **shares** (also called stock). If you own one share, you own a tiny fraction of that company: its buildings, products, brand and future profits.
Companies sell shares to raise money to grow. The first time a company sells shares to the public is called an IPO, or initial public offering. After that, shares mostly trade between investors.

sections.heading: How shareholders can make money
body: There are two main ways. First, the share price can rise if the company becomes more valuable or investors become more optimistic about it. Second, some companies pay part of their profits to shareholders as **dividends**.

There is also a downside. If the company struggles, the price can fall. If it goes bankrupt, shareholders are last in line and often get nothing. Your loss is limited to what you put in, though: you can't owe more than you paid for a share you bought outright.

sections.heading: Shareholder rights
body: Shareholders usually get a vote on big decisions, such as electing the board of directors, roughly one vote per share. In practice, small investors have very little say. The real benefit is owning a claim on the company's success.

example.title: Your slice in numbers
body: Imagine a pizza company split into 1,000,000 shares. You buy 100 shares at $20 each, spending $2,000. You own 100 / 1,000,000 = 0.01% of the company.

If the company grows and the share price rises to $25, your shares are worth $2,500, a $500 gain. If the price drops to $15, they are worth $1,500. Nothing is gained or lost until you sell, but the value is real either way.

key_terms.definition: A unit of ownership in a company.
Initial public offering: the first time a company sells its shares to the public.
Someone who owns shares in a company.

lessons.takeaway: A share is part-ownership of a real business, and its value rises and falls with that business's prospects.
lessons.try_it: Open any company card in the app and find its market cap and share price. You now know what one share represents.

quiz.question: What do you own when you buy one share of a company?
options: A loan you've made to the company
A tiny fraction of the company itself
A guaranteed slice of next year's profits
A coupon for the company's products
quiz.explanation: A share is a unit of ownership. A loan to a company is a bond, which is a different thing.

quiz.question: If a company you own shares in goes bankrupt, what typically happens to shareholders?
options: They are last in line and often get little or nothing
quiz.explanation: Lenders and other creditors get paid before shareholders. But shareholders can't lose more than they invested.

quiz.question: Which is a way shareholders can earn money?
options: Dividends or a rising share price
Monthly interest guaranteed by the company
quiz.explanation: Shareholders profit when the price rises or when the company pays dividends. Neither is guaranteed.

lessons.title: How buying and selling actually works
lessons.hook: Behind every trade there is a buyer, a seller and a price they agree on.

sections.heading: Exchanges: the marketplace
body: Shares trade on **stock exchanges**, which match buyers with sellers. In the US, the two biggest are the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and Nasdaq. Regular trading runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time on weekdays, except holidays. Other countries have their own exchanges, like London, Tokyo or Mumbai.
You don't go to the exchange yourself. You use a **broker**, an app or firm that sends your order to the market. For every share you buy, someone else is selling it.

sections.heading: Bid and ask
body: At any moment, buyers post how much they will pay (the **bid**) and sellers post how much they want (the **ask**). The ask is a bit higher than the bid. The gap is the spread.
For huge, popular companies the spread is often just a cent. For small or rarely traded stocks it can be much wider, which is a hidden cost when you trade.

sections.heading: Market vs limit orders
body: A **market order** says: buy or sell right now at the best available price. It almost always fills fast, but in a fast-moving market the price you get can differ from the price you saw.
A **limit order** says: buy only at this price or lower (or sell only at this price or higher). You control the price, but the order may never fill if the market doesn't reach your limit.

example.title: Reading a quote
body: A stock shows: bid $50.00, ask $50.05. A market buy order for 10 shares would typically fill around the ask: 10 x $50.05 = $500.50.
If you sold immediately with a market order, you'd get around the bid: 10 x $50.00 = $500.00. Even though the price didn't move, you'd be down $0.50. That's the spread.
A limit buy at $49.90 would wait. It fills only if a seller agrees to $49.90 or less.

key_terms.definition: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.
The gap between the bid and the ask; a small cost of trading.
An order to trade right away at the best available price.
An order to trade only at a chosen price or better.

lessons.takeaway: Market orders prioritise speed; limit orders prioritise price.
lessons.try_it: In paper trading, buy $1,000 of SPY. Remember that orders fill at the next price update, so compare the price you saw with the price you got.

quiz.question: A stock's bid is $20.00 and its ask is $20.10. Roughly what will you pay per share with a market buy order?
quiz.explanation: A market buy usually fills at the ask, the lowest price a seller currently accepts.

quiz.question: What is the main risk of a limit order?
options: You may pay far more than expected
It may never fill if the price doesn't reach your limit
It is only allowed for professionals
It always fills at the worst price
quiz.explanation: A limit order guarantees the price or better, but not that the trade happens.

quiz.question: Why can trading a small, rarely traded stock cost more than trading a giant company?
options: Exchanges charge small companies extra tax
Small stocks can only be bought with market orders
Its spread between bid and ask is often wider
quiz.explanation: Fewer buyers and sellers usually means a wider spread, which you pay every time you trade.

lessons.title: Indexes: taking the market's temperature
lessons.hook: What people actually mean when they say 'the market is up 1% today'.

sections.heading: A basket that stands for the market
body: There are thousands of stocks, so people track **indexes**: lists of stocks combined into one number that shows how the group is doing.

The **S&P 500** follows about 500 large US companies, picked by a committee. It is weighted by size, so a giant company moves it much more than a smaller one. Many people treat it as shorthand for 'the US stock market'.

The **Nasdaq Composite** includes the thousands of stocks listed on the Nasdaq exchange and leans heavily toward technology. The **Dow Jones Industrial Average** (the Dow) tracks just 30 big companies and is weighted by share price, an older method, so a stock with a higher price moves it more regardless of company size.

sections.heading: What 'up 1%' means
body: When the news says 'the S&P 500 rose 1% today', it means the index closed 1% higher than its previous close. Some stocks inside it fell; on balance, the group rose.
Index points can mislead. A 400-point move in the Dow sounds dramatic, but the percentage is what matters. The bigger the index number, the more points a 1% move is.

sections.heading: Other countries
body: Most markets have a headline index: the FTSE 100 in the UK, the Nikkei 225 in Japan, the Nifty 50 in India. Global indexes combine many countries.

example.title: Points vs percent
body: Suppose the Dow is at 40,000 and rises 400 points. That is 400 / 40,000 = 1%.
If the S&P 500 is at 5,000 and rises 50 points, that is also 1%. Same move, very different-sounding point numbers. (These index levels are illustrative.)

key_terms.definition: A combined measure of a group of stocks that shows how that group is performing.
An index of about 500 large US companies, weighted by company size.
An index of 30 large US companies, weighted by share price.
An index of the stocks listed on the Nasdaq exchange, heavy in technology.

lessons.takeaway: An index is the market's thermometer, and the percentage change matters more than the points.
lessons.try_it: On today's page, tap the (i) on the S&P 500 and Dow tiles. Compare their percentage moves, not their point moves.

quiz.question: The S&P 500 rises 1% today. What does that mean?
options: The index closed 1% above its previous close
quiz.explanation: An index move reflects the combined result. Some stocks rise and some fall; the overall group rose 1%.

quiz.question: The Dow rises 300 points while a smaller index rises 30 points. What can you conclude?
options: The Dow had a much better day
The smaller index had a better day
Nothing, until you compare percentage changes
quiz.explanation: Points depend on the index's level. Only the percentage move lets you compare.

quiz.question: How is the S&P 500 different from the Dow?
options: The S&P 500 has about 500 companies weighted by size; the Dow has 30 weighted by share price
The S&P 500 only includes tech companies
quiz.explanation: The S&P 500 is broader and weighted by company value, which is why many treat it as the better gauge of the US market.

lessons.title: Why stock prices move
lessons.hook: Prices move on surprises: news that changes what investors expect.

sections.heading: Price = what people expect
body: A share's price reflects what investors collectively expect about a company's future profits, and how much they are willing to pay for them today. When expectations change, the price changes.
That is why a company can report record profits and its stock still falls: investors had expected even more. Markets react to the gap between reality and expectations, not to good or bad news alone.

sections.heading: The big drivers
body: **Earnings**: how much profit a company makes and what it says about the future. **Expectations**: the forecasts already baked into the price. Interest rates: when rates rise, safe savings and bonds pay more, so stocks have more competition, and future profits are worth less in today's money. Higher rates can also slow the economy. Falling rates tend to work the other way.

**News and events**: new products, lawsuits, elections, wars, economic reports like jobs or inflation numbers. **Mood**: fear and greed can push prices further than the facts justify, in either direction.

sections.heading: Short-term noise, long-term signal
body: Day to day, prices bounce on news and emotion. Over many years, a company's price tends to follow its actual ability to grow profits, though with no guarantee and plenty of exceptions.

example.title: Good news, falling price
body: Analysts expect a company to earn $2.00 per share this quarter. It reports $1.90, up from $1.50 a year ago, a 27% increase.

Growth is strong, but it fell short of the $2.00 expectation by 5%. The stock may well drop, because the price had already assumed $2.00. Real-world reactions vary, but this gap between result and expectation is often what moves prices.

key_terms.definition: What investors already predict will happen, which is built into today's price.
A company's profit over a period, usually reported every quarter in the US.
The cost of borrowing money. Changes in rates affect how attractive stocks are versus safer options.

lessons.takeaway: Prices move when reality differs from what was expected.
lessons.try_it: Play the prediction game: pick a stock with an earnings date coming up and call it up or down for tomorrow. Write down why, and check if expectations played a part.

quiz.question: A company reports higher profits than last year, but the stock falls. What's the most likely reason?
options: Results fell short of what investors expected
Stocks can't rise on earnings day
quiz.explanation: Prices already reflect expectations. Missing them can push the price down even if results improved.

quiz.question: How do rising interest rates tend to affect stocks?
options: They usually help, because companies earn interest
They often weigh on stocks, because safer options pay more and future profits are worth less today
quiz.explanation: Higher rates raise the bar stocks must beat and reduce today's value of future profits. The effect isn't automatic, but it is a common pressure.

quiz.question: Over many years, what tends to matter most for a company's share price?
options: How many people talk about it online
quiz.explanation: Short-term moves are noisy, but long-term prices tend to track business results, though not perfectly.

lessons.title: Bull markets, bear markets and volatility
lessons.hook: Markets go through seasons. Knowing the names helps you stay calm.

sections.heading: Bulls and bears
body: A **bull market** is a long stretch of rising prices and optimism. A **bear market** is commonly defined as a fall of 20% or more from a recent high. A drop of 10% or more is often called a correction. These are informal rules of thumb, not official definitions.

Historically, US bull markets have lasted much longer than bear markets on average, but bear markets do happen, sometimes more than once a decade, and nobody can reliably predict when one starts or ends.

sections.heading: Volatility is normal
body: **Volatility** is how much prices swing. Even in good years, the stock market usually has a noticeable dip at some point, and drops of 10% or more within a single year are common. Swings are the price of admission for the higher long-run growth stocks have offered.

sections.heading: The VIX: the 'fear gauge'
body: The **VIX** is an index that estimates how much investors expect the S&P 500 to swing over the next 30 days, based on prices of options (contracts people use to bet on or protect against moves). When investors are nervous, they pay more for protection and the VIX rises.

In calm periods the VIX often sits in the teens. In panics it has spiked above 40, and at the extremes of 2008 and 2020, above 80. A high VIX means big moves are expected, not which direction they'll go.

example.title: Recovering from a drop
body: A portfolio worth $10,000 falls 20% to $8,000. To get back to $10,000, it needs to gain $2,000 on $8,000, which is 25%, not 20%.
After a 50% fall ($10,000 to $5,000), it needs a 100% gain to recover. That's why big drops feel so painful, and why staying invested through recoveries matters.

key_terms.definition: A long period of rising prices and optimism.
Commonly, a fall of 20% or more from a recent high.
Commonly, a fall of 10% or more from a recent high.
An index of expected S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days, often called the fear gauge.

lessons.takeaway: Drops and swings are a normal part of investing, not a sign something is broken.
lessons.try_it: Check the Market mood gauge on today's page. Is the market feeling fearful or greedy? Look back in a week to see whether the mood shifted.

quiz.question: The S&P 500 is 12% below its recent high. What is this commonly called?
quiz.explanation: A 10% to 20% fall is commonly called a correction; 20% or more is commonly called a bear market.

quiz.question: The VIX jumps sharply. What does that tell you?
options: Investors expect bigger price swings ahead
quiz.explanation: The VIX measures expected volatility, not direction. Prices could swing either way.

quiz.question: Your investment falls 20%. What gain do you need to get back to where you started?
quiz.explanation: After falling from $100 to $80, you need $20 on $80, which is a 25% gain.

units.title: Ways to invest
units.blurb: Funds, fees, bonds, building a mix and dividends.

lessons.title: Index funds and ETFs: buying the whole basket
lessons.hook: Instead of picking one needle, you can buy the whole haystack.

sections.heading: What a fund is
body: A **fund** pools money from many investors and buys many investments at once. With one purchase you can own a small slice of hundreds or thousands of companies.

An **index fund** simply tries to match an index, such as the S&P 500, by holding the same stocks in the same proportions. No one is trying to pick winners, which keeps costs low. Funds where managers pick investments are called **actively managed** funds; research has repeatedly found that most of them trail their index over long periods, especially after fees.

sections.heading: ETFs vs mutual funds
body: An **ETF** (exchange-traded fund) trades on an exchange like a stock: its price moves during the day and you buy it through a broker. A traditional **mutual fund** is priced once a day after the market closes. Both can be index funds. The differences are mostly about how you buy them, minimum investments and, in the US, some tax details.

SPY, VTI and QQQ, which you can trade in the app's paper trading, are ETFs that track the S&P 500, the whole US market and the Nasdaq-100 respectively. Mentioning them is not a recommendation; they are just well-known examples.

sections.heading: The trade-offs
body: Index funds give you the market's return, minus small fees. That means you'll never beat the market, but you're unlikely to fall far behind it. You also get whatever the index holds, including its booms and busts. A narrow index, like one sector, is less diversified than a broad one.

example.title: One share vs one fund
body: Put $1,000 in one company's stock. If it falls 50% you have $500.

Put $1,000 in a fund holding 500 companies, each a small slice. If one company falls 50% and it was 1% of the fund, that costs you about $5 (1% of $1,000 is $10, half of which is lost). Your result depends on how the whole group does, not one company.

key_terms.definition: A fund that tries to match the performance of an index by holding the same investments.
Exchange-traded fund: a fund that trades on an exchange like a stock.
A pooled fund usually bought directly from the fund company and priced once a day.
A fund whose managers pick investments trying to beat the market.

lessons.takeaway: An index fund lets you own a whole market in one purchase, at low cost.
lessons.try_it: In paper trading, buy $1,000 of VTI and $1,000 of QQQ. Check them over the next week and notice how differently a broad fund and a tech-heavy fund move.

quiz.question: What does an S&P 500 index fund try to do?
options: Beat the S&P 500 by picking winners
Invest only in the top 5 companies
quiz.explanation: An index fund aims to match its index, not beat it, which keeps costs low.

quiz.question: What's a key difference between an ETF and a traditional mutual fund?
options: ETFs trade during the day like stocks; mutual funds are priced once a day
ETFs are insured by the FDIC
quiz.explanation: ETFs trade on exchanges throughout the day. Both types can track indexes, and neither is FDIC insured.

quiz.question: What's a downside of an index fund?
options: You must research every company yourself
It is guaranteed to lose money
It is only available to institutions
You get the market's ups and downs, and won't beat the market
quiz.explanation: An index fund rides the market in both directions and, by design, won't outperform it.

lessons.title: Fees: the small number that eats big money
lessons.hook: A 1% fee sounds tiny. Over decades it can cost you a fortune.

sections.heading: What you pay
body: Funds charge an **expense ratio**: a yearly fee shown as a percentage of what you have invested. It is taken out of the fund automatically, so you never see a bill, which makes it easy to ignore.

A 0.05% expense ratio means $5 a year for every $10,000 invested. A 1% expense ratio means $100 a year per $10,000. Broad index funds often charge very little; many actively managed funds and financial advisers charge 1% or more. There can also be trading commissions, account fees and the bid-ask spread.

sections.heading: Why fees compound
body: Fees don't just take a slice each year. The money they take can no longer grow for you. So a fee gap compounds, just like returns do, and over decades it can add up to a big share of your final balance.

Returns are uncertain, but fees are certain. That's why, all else being equal, lower costs are one of the few things in investing that reliably help. A higher fee can be worth it if you truly get something valuable for it, like good advice that keeps you on track, but it should be a conscious choice.

sections.heading: Where to find it
body: Every fund publishes its expense ratio in its fact sheet and prospectus. Look for it before you buy. Fee rules and disclosure vary by country, but the maths is the same everywhere.

example.title: 1% vs 0.05% over 30 years (illustrative)
body: Invest $10,000 once. Assume the investments return 7% a year before fees, as a simple illustration.
With a 0.05% fee, you keep 6.95% a year. After 30 years: about $75,000.
With a 1% fee, you keep 6% a year. After 30 years: about $57,400.
Same investments, same market. The higher fee costs about $17,600, nearly twice the original $10,000.

key_terms.definition: A fund's yearly fee as a percentage of your investment, taken out automatically.
A fee charged for making a trade. Many brokers now charge none for stocks and ETFs, but check.
The official document describing a fund, including its fees, goals and risks.

lessons.takeaway: Fees are one of the few things you control, and small differences compound into big ones.
lessons.try_it: Look up 'expense ratio' in the glossary. Then calculate: what would a 1% fee cost per year on $5,000? (Answer: $50.)

quiz.question: A fund has a 0.20% expense ratio and you have $10,000 in it. What's the yearly fee?
Why does a 1% fee gap matter so much over 30 years?
options: The money taken by fees can no longer grow, so the gap compounds
Fees are charged only at the end
quiz.explanation: Every dollar paid in fees also loses all its future growth, so the difference snowballs.

quiz.question: Which is the most accurate statement about fees?
options: Fees only matter for large accounts
Expense ratios are billed separately each month
Returns are uncertain, but fees are a certain cost
quiz.explanation: You can't control returns, but you can know and control costs. Higher fees don't guarantee better results.

lessons.title: Bonds: lending your money
lessons.hook: Why bond prices fall when interest rates rise, in one simple example.

sections.heading: A bond is a loan
body: When you buy a **bond**, you lend money to a government or company. In return, they usually pay you regular interest (the **coupon**) and promise to repay the original amount (the face value) on a set date (maturity).

US Treasury bonds are backed by the US government and considered very safe from default. Corporate bonds pay more, because companies are more likely to fail to repay. Bonds from borrowers with a higher risk of default, rated below 'investment grade', are called high-yield or junk bonds.

sections.heading: Yield
body: A bond's **yield** is the return you'd earn if you bought it at today's price and held it to maturity. When you see 'the 10-year Treasury yield', that is the yield on US government debt maturing in 10 years. It is closely watched because it influences mortgage rates and many other borrowing costs.

sections.heading: Why prices fall when rates rise
body: Imagine you own a bond paying 3%. Then new bonds start paying 5%. Nobody will pay full price for your 3% bond when they could get 5% elsewhere, so its price has to drop until its yield matches the market. When rates fall, the opposite happens and older, higher-paying bonds become more valuable.

The longer until a bond matures, the more its price moves when rates change. Short-term bonds barely budge; long-term bonds can swing a lot. If you hold a high-quality bond to maturity, you still get the full face value back, as long as the issuer doesn't default.

sections.heading: Bonds in a portfolio
body: Bonds have usually swung less than stocks and paid steadier income, so people often use them to soften a portfolio's ups and downs. But they are not risk-free: inflation, rising rates and defaults can all hurt.

example.title: A one-year bond when rates change
body: A bond will pay you $1,030 in one year: $1,000 face value plus $30 interest (a 3% coupon).
If new one-year bonds suddenly pay 5%, what would a buyer pay for your bond? The price at which $1,030 is a 5% gain: $1,030 / 1.05 = about $981. Your bond's price fell about $19.
If instead rates fell to 1%, buyers would pay $1,030 / 1.01 = about $1,020. Your bond rose in value.

key_terms.definition: A loan to a government or company that pays interest and returns your money at maturity.
The interest a bond pays, usually as a fixed percentage of its face value.
The return you'd earn buying a bond at today's price and holding it to maturity.
The date when a bond's face value is repaid.

lessons.takeaway: Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.
lessons.try_it: On today's page, tap the (i) on the 10-yr Treasury tile. If the yield went up today, what likely happened to the prices of existing bonds?

quiz.question: Interest rates rise sharply. What tends to happen to the price of a bond you already own?
quiz.explanation: New bonds pay more, so your lower-paying bond must drop in price to compete.

quiz.question: Which bond's price is likely to move most when rates change?
quiz.explanation: The longer the time to maturity, the more sensitive a bond's price is to interest rate changes.

quiz.question: Why do corporate bonds usually pay higher interest than US Treasury bonds?
options: Companies are more likely than the US government to fail to repay
Companies are required by law to pay more
quiz.explanation: Higher default risk means lenders demand a higher return to compensate.

lessons.title: Diversification and asset allocation
lessons.hook: Don't put all your eggs in one basket, and choose the right mix of baskets.

sections.heading: Diversification
body: **Diversification** means spreading your money across many different investments so that one disaster doesn't sink you. If you own one company and it fails, you lose a lot. If you own 500 and one fails, you barely notice.

Diversification reduces the risk tied to individual companies or industries. It cannot remove market risk: when the whole market falls, a diversified portfolio usually falls too, just less dramatically than the worst single stocks. It is about avoiding wipeouts, not avoiding all losses.

sections.heading: Asset allocation
body: **Asset allocation** is how you split money between broad types of investments, mainly stocks, bonds and cash. It is one of the biggest drivers of how much your portfolio swings.

More stocks means more growth potential and bigger swings. More bonds and cash means a smoother ride and usually lower long-run growth. People with long time horizons often hold more stocks; people who need the money sooner often hold more bonds and cash. There is no single right mix.

sections.heading: Staying on track
body: Over time, your mix drifts as some investments grow faster. **Rebalancing** means occasionally moving money back to your chosen mix. Some people use target-date funds, which hold a mix of stocks and bonds and gradually become more conservative as a chosen year approaches. They are convenient, but check their fees and whether their mix suits you.

example.title: Two mixes in a bad year (illustrative)
body: Suppose stocks fall 30% and bonds rise 2% in a year.
Portfolio A: $10,000 all in stocks becomes $7,000, a 30% loss.
Portfolio B: $6,000 stocks and $4,000 bonds. Stocks become $4,200, bonds become $4,080. Total $8,280, a 17.2% loss.
In a strong year for stocks, A would usually come out ahead. The mix decides the ride.

key_terms.definition: Spreading money across many investments to reduce the damage any one can do.
How you divide money among stocks, bonds and cash.
Adjusting your holdings back to your chosen mix after the market shifts it.
A fund that mixes stocks and bonds and becomes more conservative as a target year nears.

lessons.takeaway: Diversification protects you from single disasters; asset allocation sets how bumpy your ride will be.
lessons.try_it: In paper trading, put your virtual money into a mix you choose, say part SPY and part a single big company. After a week, compare how each piece moved.

quiz.question: What risk can diversification NOT eliminate?
options: The risk of one company going bankrupt
The risk of one industry struggling
The risk of the whole market falling
The risk of a single CEO scandal
quiz.explanation: Spreading across many stocks reduces company-specific risk, but a broad market decline affects nearly everything.

quiz.question: Using this lesson's example numbers, why did Portfolio B lose less than Portfolio A?
options: B held some bonds, which rose while stocks fell
quiz.explanation: B's bonds cushioned the stock loss. That cushion also means B would usually trail A in strong stock years.

quiz.question: What is rebalancing?
options: Selling everything when the market falls
Moving money back to your chosen mix after it drifts
quiz.explanation: Rebalancing keeps your risk level where you intended as different investments grow at different speeds.

lessons.title: Dividends: getting paid to own
lessons.hook: Some companies send you cash just for owning their shares. Here's how it really works.

sections.heading: What a dividend is
body: A **dividend** is a payment a company makes to shareholders, usually from its profits. Many US companies that pay dividends do so every quarter. Not all companies pay them: many fast-growing companies prefer to reinvest profits in the business instead.
The **dividend yield** is the yearly dividend divided by the share price. A $100 stock paying $3 a year has a 3% yield.

sections.heading: Dividends aren't free money
body: When a dividend is paid, cash leaves the company, so the company is worth a little less. That's why a stock's price typically drops by about the dividend amount on the **ex-dividend date**, the cutoff for qualifying. You must own the shares before that date to get the payment.
Dividends are one way a company returns value; a rising share price is another. What matters is your total return: price change plus dividends.

sections.heading: Watch out for very high yields
body: A very high yield can be a warning sign. Yield rises when the price falls, so a sky-high yield sometimes means investors fear the company is in trouble and might cut the dividend. Dividends are never guaranteed and can be reduced or stopped.
You can usually choose to **reinvest dividends** automatically, buying more shares, which lets compounding work. In taxable accounts, dividends are usually taxed, and rules differ by country.

example.title: Calculating income and total return
body: You own 50 shares of a $40 stock: $2,000 invested. It pays $0.40 per share each quarter, which is $1.60 a year.
Yearly dividends: 50 x $1.60 = $80. Dividend yield: $1.60 / $40 = 4%.
If the price also rises to $42 over the year, your shares gain $100. Total return: $100 + $80 = $180, or 9% of $2,000.

key_terms.definition: A cash payment from a company to its shareholders.
The yearly dividend divided by the share price, shown as a percentage.
The cutoff date: you must own the shares before it to receive the next dividend.
Price change plus dividends, the full picture of what an investment earned.

lessons.takeaway: Judge an investment by total return, not dividend yield alone.
lessons.try_it: Open a few company cards and compare their dividend yields. Notice which pay none, and think about why a fast-growing company might skip dividends.

quiz.question: A stock costs $50 and pays $2 a year in dividends. What is its dividend yield?
quiz.explanation: $2 divided by $50 is 0.04, or 4%.

quiz.question: Why does a stock's price typically drop around its ex-dividend date?
options: Cash is leaving the company, so it's worth a bit less
It doesn't; prices never change on that day
quiz.explanation: The dividend is value moving from the company to shareholders, so the price adjusts by roughly that amount.

quiz.question: A stock suddenly shows a 15% dividend yield. What's a sensible first thought?
options: The price may have fallen because investors fear trouble, and the dividend could be cut
It must be a safe company
quiz.explanation: A very high yield often reflects a falling price and doubts about whether the dividend can continue.

resources.title: Topic no. 404, Dividends and other corporate distributions

units.title: Reading a company
units.blurb: The key numbers behind a business and its stock price.

lessons.title: Revenue, profit and margins
lessons.hook: The three numbers that tell you whether a business actually makes money.

sections.heading: From sales to profit
body: **Revenue** (also called sales or the top line) is all the money a company brings in from selling things. It is not profit. A lemonade stand that sells $1,000 of lemonade has $1,000 of revenue, even if lemons and cups cost $900.

Subtract the direct costs of making what you sell and you get **gross profit**. Subtract running costs like salaries, rent and marketing and you get **operating profit**. Subtract interest and taxes and you get net income (the bottom line), what's left for shareholders.

sections.heading: Margins: profit per dollar of sales
body: A **margin** is profit divided by revenue. A 20% net margin means the company keeps 20 cents of every dollar of sales as profit.

Margins differ hugely by industry. Supermarkets often run thin net margins of a few percent but sell enormous volumes. Software companies can have much higher margins because selling one more copy costs little. So compare a company's margins with its own past and with similar companies, not with everyone.

sections.heading: What to look for
body: Is revenue growing? Are margins stable, rising or shrinking? A company growing sales while margins collapse may be buying growth expensively. A company with shrinking sales but rising margins may be cutting costs, which can only go so far.

example.title: A coffee chain's year (illustrative)
body: Revenue: $10 million. Coffee beans, milk and cups: $3 million. Gross profit: $7 million, a 70% gross margin.
Salaries, rent and marketing: $5.5 million. Operating profit: $1.5 million, a 15% operating margin.
Interest and taxes: $0.5 million. Net income: $1 million, a 10% net margin. Of every $5 latte, about 50 cents ends up as profit.

key_terms.definition: All the money a company brings in from sales, before any costs.
Profit left after all costs, interest and taxes. Also called the bottom line.
Profit divided by revenue, showing how much of each sales dollar is kept as profit.

lessons.takeaway: Revenue is what comes in; profit is what's left; margins show how efficiently one turns into the other.
lessons.try_it: Open a company card and check its upcoming earnings date. When it arrives, read the digest story and look for revenue and profit figures.

quiz.question: A company has $50 million in revenue and $5 million in net income. What is its net margin?
quiz.explanation: $5 million divided by $50 million is 0.10, or 10%.

quiz.question: Why can't you judge a company by revenue alone?
options: Revenue is the same as profit
High revenue can still come with high costs and little or no profit
quiz.explanation: Revenue is before costs. A company can sell a lot and still lose money.

quiz.question: A supermarket has a 3% net margin and a software company has a 25% net margin. What can you conclude?
options: Margins vary by industry, so compare companies with similar businesses
The software company is a better investment
The supermarket must be losing money
quiz.explanation: Different industries have very different cost structures. Margins are most useful compared with peers and with the company's own history.

lessons.title: EPS, P/E and market cap
lessons.hook: How to tell whether a stock is 'expensive', and why a high price doesn't mean big.

sections.heading: Market cap: the size of the company
body: **Market capitalisation** (market cap) is the total value of all a company's shares: share price times number of shares. It tells you how big the market thinks the company is.
The share price alone tells you almost nothing about size. A $500 stock can belong to a smaller company than a $50 stock, if the $50 company has many more shares.

sections.heading: EPS: profit per share
body: **Earnings per share** (EPS) is net income divided by the number of shares. If a company earns $1 billion and has 500 million shares, its EPS is $2. It lets you compare profit growth over time even as the number of shares changes.

sections.heading: P/E: the price tag on profits
body: The **price-to-earnings ratio** (P/E) is the share price divided by EPS. A stock at $40 with EPS of $2 has a P/E of 20: investors are paying $20 for every $1 of yearly profit. Trailing P/E uses the past year's earnings; forward P/E uses forecasts.

A high P/E usually means investors expect strong growth. A low P/E can mean a bargain, or that investors expect trouble. P/E doesn't work for companies with no profits, and it varies by industry and over time. It's a starting question, not an answer.

example.title: Comparing two companies
body: Company A: share price $200, 100 million shares, net income $1 billion. Market cap = $200 x 100 million = $20 billion. EPS = $1 billion / 100 million = $10. P/E = $200 / $10 = 20.
Company B: share price $50, 1 billion shares, net income $1 billion. Market cap = $50 billion. EPS = $1. P/E = 50.
B has the lower share price but is the bigger company, and investors pay much more for each dollar of its profit, likely because they expect faster growth.

key_terms.definition: Share price times number of shares: the market's total value for a company.
Earnings per share: net income divided by the number of shares.
Share price divided by earnings per share: how much investors pay for $1 of yearly profit.

lessons.takeaway: Market cap shows size, EPS shows profit per share, and P/E shows how much investors are paying for those profits.
lessons.try_it: Open two company cards and compare their market cap and P/E. Which does the market expect to grow faster, and why might that be?

quiz.question: A stock trades at $60 and its EPS is $3. What is its P/E ratio?
quiz.explanation: P/E is price divided by EPS: $60 / $3 = 20.

quiz.question: Stock X costs $300 per share and stock Y costs $30. What do you know about which company is bigger?
options: Nothing yet; you need the number of shares to compare market caps
quiz.explanation: Size is market cap, which depends on both price and the number of shares.

quiz.question: A company has a very high P/E. What does that usually suggest?
options: The stock is about to fall
quiz.explanation: A high P/E usually reflects high growth expectations. Whether those expectations are justified is the real question.

resources.title: CFA Program Level I exam (topics overview)

lessons.title: Earnings reports: beats, misses and 'adjusted' numbers
lessons.hook: How to read earnings-day headlines, and why there are two versions of profit.

sections.heading: Report card season
body: US public companies report results every quarter, plus a fuller annual report, filed with the SEC (the US market regulator). Companies in some other countries report every six months. Around each report, you'll see headlines about the company beating or missing estimates.

**Estimates** (or consensus) are the average forecasts of analysts who follow the company. A **beat** means results came in above estimates; a miss means below. As you learned, prices react to the surprise, not just the result.

sections.heading: Guidance: the forward look
body: Many companies also give **guidance**: their own forecast for the next quarter or year. Guidance often moves the stock more than the results themselves. A company can beat this quarter and still fall if it lowers its outlook.

sections.heading: GAAP vs adjusted earnings
body: In the US, official results follow **GAAP** (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles), a standard rulebook. Many other countries use a similar rulebook called IFRS. Many companies also report **adjusted** (non-GAAP) earnings that leave out certain costs, such as restructuring charges or stock-based pay for employees.

Adjusted numbers can help show the ongoing business by stripping out one-off events. But companies choose the adjustments, and they almost always make profits look bigger. Stock-based pay, for example, is a real cost to shareholders. US rules require companies to show how adjusted numbers reconcile to GAAP, so you can compare. A big, persistent gap between the two is worth questioning.

example.title: Same quarter, two profits
body: A company reports GAAP net income of $80 million. It adds back $30 million of stock-based pay and $10 million of restructuring costs, giving adjusted net income of $120 million, 50% higher.
With 100 million shares, GAAP EPS is $0.80 and adjusted EPS is $1.20. If analysts expected $1.10 adjusted, headlines will say it beat. The GAAP picture is less rosy, and both are true at once.

key_terms.definition: The average forecast of analysts for a company's results.
A company's own forecast for upcoming results.
The standard US accounting rules for official financial results.
Company-chosen profit figures that exclude certain costs; also called non-GAAP.

lessons.takeaway: Look at both the headline 'beat' and the guidance, and check how far adjusted earnings sit from GAAP.
lessons.try_it: Find a company card with an earnings date this week. After it reports, read the digest story and note: beat or miss, and did guidance go up or down?

quiz.question: A company beats this quarter's estimates but cuts its forecast for next year. What might happen to the stock?
options: It must rise because it beat
It could fall, because guidance often matters more than the past quarter
quiz.explanation: Investors care about the future. Lowered guidance can outweigh a good quarter.

quiz.question: Why should you be careful with adjusted earnings?
options: They are always lower than GAAP
Companies choose what to exclude, and the result usually looks better
quiz.explanation: Adjustments can be informative, but they are chosen by the company and tend to flatter profits.

quiz.question: GAAP EPS is $0.80 and adjusted EPS is $1.20. Which is true?
options: Both can be accurate; they measure profit under different rules
One of them must be fraud
Adjusted EPS is the only official number
quiz.explanation: GAAP is the official standard; adjusted EPS excludes some costs. Both can be correct, but they answer different questions.

lessons.title: The balance sheet in plain English
lessons.hook: What a company owns, what it owes, and what's left for shareholders.

sections.heading: A snapshot
body: A **balance sheet** is a snapshot of a company's finances on one day. It has three parts. **Assets**: what the company owns, like cash, buildings, equipment, inventory and money customers owe it. Liabilities: what it owes, like loans, bonds and bills to suppliers. Shareholders' equity: what's left over for owners.
It always balances: assets = liabilities + equity. Think of a house: if your home is worth $400,000 and your mortgage is $300,000, your equity is $100,000.

sections.heading: What to look for
body: **Cash vs debt**: lots of cash and little debt gives a company room to survive bad times. Heavy debt is not automatically bad, but it means interest payments must be made even in tough years, and rising rates make new borrowing pricier.

**Short-term health**: compare current assets (cash and things that turn into cash within a year) with current liabilities (bills due within a year). If short-term bills far exceed short-term resources, the company may struggle to pay them.

sections.heading: Its limits
body: The balance sheet doesn't show whether a company is profitable; that's the income statement, which covers revenue and profit. It also tends to undervalue things like brands and know-how. Use it alongside profit and cash flow, not alone.

example.title: Reading a simple balance sheet
body: A company has $500 million in assets: $100 million cash, $150 million inventory and customer bills, $250 million buildings and equipment.
It owes $300 million: $80 million in bills due this year and a $220 million long-term loan. Equity = $500 million - $300 million = $200 million.
Current assets ($100m cash + $150m inventory and customer bills = $250m) comfortably exceed current liabilities ($80m), so short-term bills look manageable.

key_terms.definition: Everything a company owns that has value.
Everything a company owes to others.
Assets minus liabilities: the owners' share of the company on paper.
A snapshot of what a company owns and owes on a given date.

lessons.takeaway: Assets minus liabilities equals equity, and a strong balance sheet helps a company survive hard times.
lessons.try_it: Reflection: write your own mini balance sheet. List what you own and what you owe. What's your equity?

quiz.question: A company has $900 million in assets and $600 million in liabilities. What is its shareholders' equity?
quiz.explanation: Equity equals assets minus liabilities: $900 million minus $600 million is $300 million.

quiz.question: Which question can the balance sheet alone NOT answer?
options: How much cash the company has
Whether it made a profit last year
What it owes within the next year
quiz.explanation: Profit comes from the income statement. The balance sheet is a snapshot of what's owned and owed.

quiz.question: Why might heavy debt be a risk for a company?
options: Interest must be paid even in bad years, and refinancing can get more expensive
quiz.explanation: Debt creates fixed obligations. In a downturn or when rates rise, those can strain a company.

units.title: Smart habits
units.blurb: The habits, accounts and mindset that matter most over a lifetime.

lessons.title: Steady wins: dollar-cost averaging and time in the market
lessons.hook: Why investing regularly and staying put usually beats trying to outsmart the market.

sections.heading: Dollar-cost averaging
body: **Dollar-cost averaging** (DCA) means investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule, like $200 every month, no matter what prices are doing. When prices are low, your $200 buys more shares; when they're high, it buys fewer.

Many people already do this through workplace retirement plans that invest part of every paycheck. Its biggest benefit is behavioural: you don't have to decide when to invest, so fear and excitement have less say.

sections.heading: An honest comparison
body: If you already have a lump sum, studies of past market data have found that investing it all at once has more often come out ahead than spreading it out, simply because markets have risen more often than they've fallen. DCA trades some expected return for less regret if prices drop right after you invest. Both are reasonable; neither is guaranteed.

sections.heading: Time in the market vs timing it
body: **Market timing** means trying to jump out before drops and back in before rises. It sounds clever, but you have to be right twice: when to get out and when to get back in. Many of the market's best days have come close to its worst days, often during scary periods when it feels safest to be out. Missing even a handful of those best days can noticeably lower long-run returns.
Staying invested through the ups and downs, with money you won't need soon, has historically been a more reliable approach than trying to predict them.

example.title: DCA through a dip
body: You invest $100 a month for three months. The fund's price is $10, then $5, then $10.
Month 1: 10 shares. Month 2: 20 shares. Month 3: 10 shares. Total: 40 shares for $300, an average cost of $7.50 per share.
The average price over those months was about $8.33, but your average cost was lower, because your fixed amount bought more when the price was low. At $10, your 40 shares are worth $400.

key_terms.definition: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price.
Investing a large amount all at once.
Trying to buy and sell based on predictions of short-term market moves.

lessons.takeaway: A steady habit and patience beat trying to guess the market's next move.
lessons.try_it: In paper trading, pick one ETF and buy the same dollar amount every week for a month. Compare your average cost with the price on the last day.

quiz.question: You invest $300 per month. The price is $30 one month and $15 the next. How many shares do you buy in total?
quiz.explanation: $300 / $30 = 10 shares, and $300 / $15 = 20 shares, for 30 shares in total.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of dollar-cost averaging?
options: It always beats investing a lump sum
It builds a habit and takes emotion out of deciding when to invest
It avoids all losses in a falling market
quiz.explanation: DCA's strength is discipline and reduced regret, not guaranteed higher returns.

quiz.question: Why is market timing so hard?
options: You have to be right about both when to get out and when to get back in
The market only moves once a year
quiz.explanation: Getting one call right isn't enough, and the best days often come right after the worst ones.

lessons.title: Your brain on money: common traps
lessons.hook: The biggest risk to your investments is often the person in the mirror.

sections.heading: Fear and greed
body: **FOMO** (fear of missing out) is the urge to pile in after something has already shot up, because everyone else seems to be getting rich. It often leads people to buy near the top.

**Panic selling** is the opposite: selling after a big drop to make the pain stop. It locks in losses and often means missing the recovery. Together, these lead to buying high and selling low, the reverse of what investors want.

sections.heading: Overconfidence
body: After a few wins, it's easy to feel like an expert. **Overconfidence** leads people to trade too often, bet too much on single ideas and underestimate risk. Frequent trading also adds costs and, in taxable accounts, taxes. Luck in a rising market can feel exactly like skill.

sections.heading: Home bias and other blind spots
body: **Home bias** is holding mostly investments from your own country, or even your own employer, because they feel familiar. The US is a large part of the world stock market, but far from all of it, and for investors in smaller countries, home bias can mean very concentrated risk. Holding lots of your employer's stock is double exposure: your job and your savings depend on the same company.

Other common traps: anchoring (fixating on the price you paid) and loss aversion (research suggests a loss can feel about twice as painful as an equal gain feels good, so people hold losers too long hoping to break even).

example.title: The cost of buying high and selling low (illustrative)
body: Jordan buys $5,000 of a hot stock after it doubled, at $100 a share: 50 shares.
It falls 40% to $60. Jordan panics and sells: 50 x $60 = $3,000, a $2,000 loss.

A year later it's back at $90. Holding would have meant a $500 paper loss instead of a $2,000 realised one. The price path was the same; the behaviour made the difference. (Of course, some stocks never recover, which is another reason to diversify.)

key_terms.definition: Fear of missing out: the urge to buy something because others are profiting from it.
Selling investments in fear after a drop, often locking in losses.
Overestimating your own skill or knowledge, often after a few wins.
Favouring investments from your own country or employer because they feel familiar.

lessons.takeaway: Have a plan before emotions show up, and stick to it when they do.
lessons.try_it: Reflection: write one sentence describing what you'll do the next time the market drops 20%. Keep it somewhere you'll see it.

quiz.question: A stock has tripled in a month and everyone online is talking about it. You feel an urge to buy right now. Which trap is this?
quiz.explanation: The urge to jump in because others seem to be profiting is fear of missing out.

quiz.question: Why can holding lots of your employer's stock be risky?
options: Your job and your savings depend on the same company
quiz.explanation: If the company struggles, you could lose your income and your savings at the same time.

quiz.question: After a string of winning trades, someone starts trading every day with bigger amounts. What trap might they be falling into?
quiz.explanation: Early wins, often helped by luck, can create overconfidence, leading to more risk and trading costs.

lessons.title: Spotting hype and scams
lessons.hook: If it sounds too good to be true, it almost always is.

sections.heading: Red flags
body: **'Guaranteed' high returns**: real investments with high return potential carry risk. Anyone guaranteeing big returns is either mistaken or lying. **Pressure to act now**: 'only today', 'don't tell anyone'. Scammers rush you so you don't think or check.

**Unregistered sellers**: in the US, you can check brokers and advisers on FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's Investor.gov. Other countries have their own regulators and registers. Be wary of anyone asking you to pay in crypto, gift cards or wire transfers to strangers, and of 'mentors' you met on social media or dating apps.

sections.heading: Pump-and-dump
body: In a **pump-and-dump**, promoters buy a cheap, little-traded stock or crypto token, then hype it online with exciting claims. As new buyers rush in, the price jumps. The promoters sell at the top, the price collapses and late buyers are left with big losses. This is illegal market manipulation, but it still happens, especially with tiny stocks and new tokens.

sections.heading: Meme mania and hype
body: Sometimes crowds pile into a stock or token because of online buzz rather than the business behind it. These **meme** surges can create huge gains for some and huge losses for others, very fast. Not all hype is fraud, but when the story is mostly 'it's going up because everyone's buying', the price can fall just as fast when the buying stops.
Healthy questions: How does this make money? Who is telling me, and what do they gain? What happens if I'm wrong?

example.title: Anatomy of a pump-and-dump (illustrative)
body: A promoter buys 1 million shares of a tiny company at $0.50: cost $500,000.
After a hype campaign, the price climbs to $2.00. The promoter sells everything for $2 million, a $1.5 million profit.
Without the hype, buyers vanish and the price falls back to $0.40. Someone who bought 1,000 shares at $2.00 for $2,000 now holds $400, an 80% loss.

key_terms.definition: A scheme where promoters hype an asset to raise its price, then sell to late buyers before it collapses.
A fraud that pays earlier investors with money from newer investors instead of real profits.
A stock whose price is driven mainly by social media buzz rather than business results.

lessons.takeaway: Guaranteed returns, pressure to hurry and anonymous hype are warning signs to walk away from.
lessons.try_it: Next time a story in the digest mentions a stock jumping on online buzz, ask the three healthy questions from this lesson before forming an opinion.

quiz.question: A stranger online promises '20% a month, guaranteed' if you send crypto. What's the best read?
options: A strong sign of a scam
Safe if the website looks professional
quiz.explanation: Guaranteed high returns plus unusual payment methods are classic scam signals.

quiz.question: In a pump-and-dump, who usually loses money?
options: Late buyers who arrive after the hype
quiz.explanation: Promoters sell to the late buyers at inflated prices; when hype fades, those buyers are left with losses.

quiz.question: A tiny company's stock jumps 300% in a week on social media buzz with no news from the company. What's a sensible response?
options: Ask how the business makes money and who benefits from the hype
quiz.explanation: Questioning the story and the source protects you; chasing unexplained spikes is how many people get burned.

lessons.title: Account types and taxes: the basics
lessons.hook: Where you hold your investments can matter almost as much as what you buy.

sections.heading: Regular brokerage accounts
body: A **taxable brokerage account** is the most flexible: you can put in and take out money any time. The trade-off is taxes on dividends, interest and profits from selling.

sections.heading: Retirement accounts in the US
body: A **401(k)** is a workplace retirement plan. Money usually goes in from your paycheck before income tax, grows without yearly tax and is taxed when you withdraw it in retirement. Many employers add a **match**, extra money when you contribute; if one is offered, it's worth understanding, because it's part of your pay.

An **IRA** (individual retirement account) is one you open yourself. With a **traditional IRA**, contributions may be tax-deductible now, and withdrawals are taxed later. With a Roth IRA, you contribute money you've already paid tax on, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. Roth contributions have income limits. Many 401(k)s also offer a Roth version.

These accounts have yearly contribution limits that change, so check the current limits. Withdrawing before age 59 and a half usually means taxes plus a penalty, with some exceptions. Other countries have their own versions, such as ISAs and pensions in the UK, or TFSAs and RRSPs in Canada.

sections.heading: Capital gains in one paragraph
body: When you sell an investment for more than you paid, the profit is a **capital gain**. In the US, gains on investments held one year or less are short-term and taxed like ordinary income; gains on investments held more than a year are long-term and usually taxed at lower rates. You only owe tax when you sell (the gain is 'realised'), losses can offset gains, and none of this applies inside retirement accounts while money stays in. Rules vary by country and change over time, so check current rules or ask a tax professional.

example.title: Traditional vs Roth (illustrative, same 20% tax rate)
body: You have $1,000 of earnings to invest and pay a 20% tax rate both now and in retirement.
Traditional: the full $1,000 goes in. Say it triples to $3,000. You pay 20% on withdrawal and keep $2,400.
Roth: you pay $200 tax first and invest $800. It triples to $2,400, withdrawn tax-free. You keep $2,400.
Same result when tax rates are equal. The choice depends mainly on whether you expect your tax rate to be higher or lower later.

key_terms.definition: A US workplace retirement account, often funded from your paycheck before tax.
A US retirement account funded with after-tax money; qualified withdrawals are tax-free.
The profit from selling an investment for more than you paid.
Money an employer adds to your retirement account when you contribute.

lessons.takeaway: Account type decides when you pay tax, so know the rules before choosing where to invest.
lessons.try_it: Look up '401(k)', 'IRA' and 'Roth IRA' in the glossary. Then, reflection: does your job (or a future one) offer a retirement plan or match?

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a traditional IRA and a Roth IRA?
options: Roth IRAs can only hold bonds
Traditional: possible tax break now, taxed later. Roth: taxed now, qualified withdrawals tax-free
Traditional IRAs are only for employers
quiz.explanation: The difference is mainly when you pay tax: on the way in (Roth) or on the way out (traditional).

quiz.question: In the US, you sell a stock for a profit after holding it for 8 months. How is the gain generally treated?
options: As a short-term gain, taxed like ordinary income
As a long-term gain at lower rates
It's only taxed if you buy again
quiz.explanation: Gains on investments held one year or less are short-term and taxed at ordinary income rates.

quiz.question: Why might someone invest in a taxable brokerage account even though it has fewer tax breaks?
options: It has no taxes at all
It's flexible: no contribution limits or early-withdrawal penalties
It's required before opening an IRA
quiz.explanation: Taxable accounts trade tax advantages for flexibility, which suits goals before retirement.

lessons.title: Using the daily news without overreacting
lessons.hook: How to read market headlines like a calm, curious learner.

sections.heading: Headlines are built to grab you
body: News has to be interesting, so moves get dramatic words: 'stocks plunge', 'markets soar'. Often the actual move is 1% or 2%, which is normal. Before reacting, check the percentage and ask whether it actually changes anything about your long-term plan. Usually it doesn't.

sections.heading: Use news to learn, not to trade
body: Daily news is a great teacher. Each story is a chance to see the ideas from this course in action: an earnings beat with weak guidance, bond yields rising after an inflation report, a meme stock spiking. Ask: what was expected, what happened and why did prices react?

What news is bad at is telling you what to do with long-term money. By the time a story is public, prices have usually already moved. Reacting to every headline mostly adds stress, costs and the traps from earlier lessons.

sections.heading: A healthy daily routine
body: Read the app's **daily digest** for a few minutes. Glance at the market strip to see the S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow, 10-year Treasury and Bitcoin, and tap the (i) on anything unfamiliar. Look up new words in the glossary. Take the daily quiz to lock in what you learned. Use the prediction game and paper trading to test your ideas with virtual money, not real money.
Then close the app and get on with your day. The goal is understanding, not constant action.

example.title: Putting a 'plunge' in perspective (illustrative)
body: A headline says 'Dow plunges 600 points'. With the Dow at 40,000, that's 600 / 40,000 = 1.5%.

Suppose your broad stock fund grew from $10,000 to $11,000 over the past year. A similar 1.5% drop takes it to $10,835: down $165 today, but still up about 8.4% on the year. A bad day, not a disaster.

key_terms.definition: The tendency of dramatic news to trigger hasty decisions.
When news is already reflected in an asset's price because investors expected it.
The app's daily summary of market stories, written to help you learn.

lessons.takeaway: Read the news to understand the market, not to react to it.
lessons.try_it: Read today's digest and pick one story. In one sentence, explain which lesson from this course it connects to. Then take the daily quiz.

quiz.question: A headline says 'Stocks tumble!' What's the best first step?
options: Sell everything before it gets worse
Check the actual percentage move and whether it changes your long-term plan
quiz.explanation: Dramatic words often describe normal moves. Percentages and your time horizon give perspective.

quiz.question: Why is trading on news you just read often a poor strategy?
options: Prices have usually already moved by the time news is public
quiz.explanation: Markets react quickly to new information, so by the time you read it, the move has usually happened.

quiz.question: What is the best use of the prediction game and paper trading?
options: To test ideas and learn without risking real money
To prove you can beat the market
quiz.explanation: Virtual money lets you practise and learn from mistakes safely.
